mainTopic: Announcing and returning lost items: how the announcement developed over time, proving ownership with סימנים and witnesses against swindlers, and caring for or selling found animals.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a question about festival announcements: what if someone mixes up the festivals? The answer is that the third festival is still coming. A ברייתא then tells the history of announcing lost items. First it was three festivals in ירושלים plus seven days. After the חורבן it moved to בתי כנסיות and בתי מדרשות. When harsh rulers who took lost items for the king spread, the finder only had to tell his neighbors. A new משנה rules that a claimant needs סימנים, and a known רמאי gets nothing even with סימנים. רב יהודה and רב נחמן argue about whether the finder may name the item in his announcement. A ברייתא and a story about רב פפא's father show the later rule that a claimant must bring witnesses that he is not a רמאי. A further משנה teaches that a found animal that pays for its own food is kept, and one that only eats is sold. The גמרא sets time limits for different animals and settles two ברייתות that seem to contradict each other. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to pin down the dispute between רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא about the sale money, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Worry about mixing up the second festival with the first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a concern: someone might confuse the second festival with the first.
steps.simpleTranslation: But someone might come to confuse it with the first festival!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing its discussion of the festival announcements from the previous page. It raises a worry that a listener might mix up which festival is which.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The announcements are tied to specific festivals. If a person confuses the second festival with the first, the timing could go wrong. The challenge asks whether this mix-up breaks the system.

phrases.english: It may come to be confused with the first [festival]!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the festival-announcement discussion from the previous amud (28a).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A listener might confuse the second festival with the first, which would throw off the system.

steps.title: The third festival is still coming
steps.stepSummary: The mix-up does not matter, because the finder will still announce at the third festival.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the third festival is coming anyway!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry. Even if someone mixes up the festivals, the finder will announce again at the third festival.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The system has a built-in backup. One confusion cannot cause the owner to lose his item for good, because another announcement is still coming.

phrases.english: But the third festival is coming!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry about confusion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the problem has no real effect, because a backup announcement remains.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Confusing the festivals could make the owner miss his chance.
steps.terutzMaskana: The third festival gives another chance, so the confusion causes no harm.

steps.title: The original system: three festivals plus seven days
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that at first, a finder announced on three festivals and then for seven more days.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Originally, anyone who found a lost item would announce it on three festivals, and for seven days after the last festival. This gave the owner three days to travel home, three days to come back, and one day to announce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that begins the history of announcing lost items. It describes the original system, when everyone came to ירושלים for the festivals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seven days are carefully counted. The owner gets three days to travel home and check what he lost, three days to return, and one day to announce his claim.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the announcement system was built to give the owner a real chance to get his item back.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Originally, anyone who found a lost item
would announce it on three festivals,
and after the last festival, for seven days,
so that [the owner] can go [home] for three [days]
and return for three, and announce for one day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא about the history of announcing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Originally a finder announced on three festivals plus seven days after the last one.

steps.title: After the חורבן: announcing in shuls and study halls
steps.stepSummary: Once the בית המקדש was destroyed, the רבנן set up announcements in בתי כנסיות and בתי מדרשות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once the בית המקדש was destroyed, may it be rebuilt quickly in our days, they made a rule that finders should announce in synagogues and study halls.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues. Without festival gatherings in ירושלים, the announcements moved to places where people gather.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The festival system worked only because everyone came to ירושלים. Once that ended, the רבנן picked new public places, so the goal of reaching the owner stayed the same.

keyTerms.meaning: They instituted, set up a rule

phrases.english: Once the Temple was destroyed,
may it be rebuilt speedily in our days,
they instituted that [finders] should announce
in synagogues and study halls.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second stage of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the חורבן, announcements were made in synagogues and study halls.

steps.title: When oppressors spread: telling neighbors is enough
steps.stepSummary: When oppressors became common, the רבנן said it is enough to tell neighbors and acquaintances.
steps.simpleTranslation: And once the oppressors became many, they made a rule that the finder should let his neighbors and acquaintances know, and that is enough for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its third and final stage. Public announcing became risky, so a quieter method was put in place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule became smaller, not bigger. Instead of announcing in public, the finder only tells the people around him. The word ודיו tells us he has done his full duty.

keyTerms.meaning: Oppressors, people who take by force
And that is enough for him

steps.whatToRemember: Three stages: (1) three festivals plus seven days, (2) after the חורבן, in shuls and study halls, (3) under oppressors, just telling neighbors and acquaintances.

phrases.english: And once the oppressors became many,
they instituted that [finders] should inform
his neighbors and his acquaintances, and that suffices for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final stage of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once oppressors spread, informing neighbors and acquaintances is enough.

steps.title: Who were the oppressors?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא means by 'once the oppressors became many.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'once the oppressors became many' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to explain a phrase in the ברייתא. This question sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא never said why oppressors would make public announcing a problem. The גמרא wants to know what kind of oppression this was.

phrases.english: What is 'once the oppressors became many'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a phrase in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the phrase 'oppressors became many' refers to.

steps.title: Rulers who claimed lost items for the king
steps.stepSummary: The oppressors were governments that said every lost item belongs to the king.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The rulers] who say: a lost item belongs to the king.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The oppressors were rulers who took found items for the king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the rule makes sense. A public announcement would tell the government about the item, and the government would take it. Quietly telling neighbors avoids that.

keyTerms.meaning: A lost item goes to the king

phrases.english: Who say: a lost item [belongs] to the king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The oppressors were rulers who claimed that lost items belong to the king.

steps.title: רבי אמי and the Roman
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי found a container of coins and was nervous. A Roman told him to take it, since Romans don't claim lost items for the king the way the Persians do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי found a container of dinars. A certain Roman saw that he was nervous. He said to him: Go, take it for yourself, because we are not Persians, who say that a lost item belongs to the king.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the idea of 'a lost item belongs to the king' in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story confirms that some governments, like the Persians, really did take lost items. It also shows that not every government did this, since the Romans did not.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami found a container of dinars;
a certain Roman saw him, that he was nervous.
He said to him: Go, take it for yourself,
for we are not Persians
who say: a lost item [belongs] to the king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the explanation from step 7 in a real story.
steps.raayaObject: That some rulers, like the Persians, claimed lost items for the king.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי אמי and the Roman.

steps.title: The אבן הטוען in ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא describes a stone in ירושלים where finders announced items and owners came to claim them with סימנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: There was a 'Claimants' Stone' in ירושלים. Anyone who lost something would go there, and anyone who found something would go there. The finder stood and announced, and the owner stood, gave identifying signs, and took it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא about lost items in ירושלים. It describes a set meeting place for finders and owners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stone made the system work smoothly, because both sides knew where to go. The owner still had to prove ownership with סימנים before taking the item.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
There was a Claimants' Stone in Jerusalem.
phrases.notes: Some versions add the letter in square brackets, so read it as טוֹעִין.

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מִי שֶׁאָבְדָה לוֹ אֲבֵידָה נִפְנֶה לְשָׁם,
phrases.english: Anyone who lost an item would go there,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל מִי שֶׁמּוֹצֵא אֲבֵידָה נִפְנֶה לְשָׁם.
phrases.english: and anyone who found a lost item would go there.
This one [the finder] stands and announces,
and that one [the owner] stands, gives signs, and takes it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֶבֶן טוֹעִין הָיְתָה בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא with more detail about how lost items were handled in ירושלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In ירושלים, finders and owners met at the אבן הטוען, and the owner took the item after giving סימנים.

steps.title: The same stone mentioned in a משנה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא connects the stone to a משנה that says: go see if the אבן הטוען has been covered up.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what we learned in a משנה: Go out and see whether the Claimants' Stone has been wiped away.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ties its stone to a known משנה. This explains which stone that משנה was talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A beginner reading the משנה might not know what the אבן הטוען is. This ברייתא fills that in: it was the lost-and-found stone in ירושלים.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what we learned (in a משנה)

steps.whatToRemember: The אבן הטוען was the public lost-and-found spot in ירושלים, and it is the same stone the משנה in תענית mentions.

phrases.english: And this is what we learned:
phrases.notes: This refers to a משנה in תענית 19a.

phrases.aramaic: צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אִם נִמְחֵת אֶבֶן הַטּוֹעִ[י]ן.
phrases.english: Go out and see if the Claimants' Stone has been wiped away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects the stone from step 9 to a known משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That the אבן הטוען was a real, known place in ירושלים.

steps.title: The משנה: no סימנים means no return, and a swindler is never trusted
steps.stepSummary: A claimant who names the item but gives no סימנים does not get it. A known רמאי does not get it even with סימנים, based on the פסוק in דברים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'that's my lost item' but cannot describe its identifying marks, the finder doesn't give it to him. And a known swindler doesn't get it even if he gives the marks, because the Torah says 'until your brother seeks it.' The משנה reads this as: until you investigate your brother to see whether he is a swindler or not.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה gives two rules for when a finder may hand a lost item back to someone claiming it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rule one: just naming the type of item is not enough; the claimant must give real סימנים. Rule two: סימנים are not enough if the claimant is a known רמאי. The משנה reads 'דרש' as the finder checking the claimant, not the owner asking for his item.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה, the source text the גמרא is about to discuss
Identifying marks that prove an item belongs to you
A swindler, someone known to make false claims
Seek or investigate. Here the משנה reads it as the finder examining the claimant.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'עד דרש אחיך אתו' as 'until your brother asks for it.' The משנה reads it as 'until YOU investigate your brother,' meaning the finder checks whether the claimant is honest.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that סימנים are the normal proof of ownership, but they can be outweighed by what we know about the person claiming.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If he stated what the lost item was,
phrases.notes: He named the type of item, like 'a cloak,' but nothing more specific.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָמַר סִימָנֶיהָ – לֹא יִתֵּן לוֹ.
phrases.english: but did not state its identifying marks, he shall not give it to him.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָרַמַּאי, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמַר סִימָנֶיהָ
phrases.english: And the swindler, even though he stated its marks,
he shall not give it to him, as it is said:
"Until your brother seeks it,"
phrases.notes: דברים 22:2

phrases.english: meaning: until you investigate your brother

phrases.aramaic: אִם רַמַּאי הוּא אִם אֵינוֹ רַמַּאי.
phrases.english: whether he is a swindler or is not a swindler.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אָמַר אֶת הָאֲבֵידָה וְלֹא אָמַר סִימָנֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, moving from how lost items are announced in public to what proof a claimant needs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A claimant without סימנים does not receive the item, and a known רמאי does not receive it even with סימנים.

steps.title: How specific should the finder's announcement be?
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the finder announces only 'a lost item.' רב נחמן says he names the item, such as 'a cloak.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רב יהודה says the finder announces 'I found a lost item.' רב נחמן says he announces 'I found a cloak.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a dispute about the finder's public announcement: does he say what kind of item he found, or only that he found something? The next two steps will explain each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side argues with the משנה's rule that the claimant must give סימנים. The argument is only about how much the finder reveals up front. The more he reveals, the easier it could be for a liar to make a claim.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that follows and explains the משנה
It was stated. This introduces a dispute between אמוראים.
A lost item, said in general terms
A cloak, used here as an example of naming the specific item

phrases.english: GEMARA:
It was stated: Rav Yehuda said:
He announces "a lost item."
And Rav Nachman said:
He announces "a cloak."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the משנה's demand for סימנים by asking what the finder should reveal in his announcement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dispute: רב יהודה says announce generally ('a lost item'); רב נחמן says announce specifically ('a cloak').

steps.title: רב יהודה's reason: naming the item helps a swindler
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says announce only 'a lost item,' because naming it as a cloak invites a רמאי to make a false claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says to announce 'a lost item,' because if the finder announced 'a cloak,' we would worry that a swindler would claim it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב יהודה's view and now gives his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the finder says 'cloak,' a swindler knows exactly what to claim. He might find out from the real owner what the cloak looked like and come with the right סימנים. Keeping the announcement general makes a false claim harder.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who holds the announcement should be general
For if you say. This introduces what would go wrong under the other approach.
We are concerned; we take this risk into account

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: He announces "a lost item,"
for if you say he announces "a cloak,"
we are concerned about a swindler.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: ״אֲבֵידְתָּא״ מַכְרֵיז, דְּאִי אָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רב יהודה's side of the dispute in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The announcement should be general because of the risk of a רמאי.

steps.title: רב נחמן's reason: worrying about swindlers would never end
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says announce 'a cloak.' We don't worry about a רמאי, because if we did, the worry would have no end.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן says to announce 'a cloak.' We are not concerned about swindlers, because if we were, there would be no end to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב נחמן's view and gives his reason. He answers רב יהודה's worry head-on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן argues that the fear of swindlers has no stopping point. Even a general announcement could be exploited, since a swindler might guess the item or learn about it some other way. So the סימנים requirement is protection enough, and the finder may name the item.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who holds the finder may name the item
We are not concerned; we ignore this risk
For if so; if we accepted that reasoning
There is no end to the matter. The worry could never be fully satisfied.

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that the claimant needs סימנים. רב יהודה adds another safeguard by keeping the announcement general. רב נחמן says that extra worry about a רמאי has no limit, so it is not taken into account.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: He announces "a cloak,"
and we are not concerned about a swindler,
for if so, there is no end to the matter.
phrases.notes: Even a vague announcement can't fully stop a swindler, so this worry could never be satisfied.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר: ״גְּלִימָא״ מַכְרֵיז, לְרַמַּאי לָא חָיְישִׁינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רב נחמן's reasoning, which directly rejects the swindler concern raised by רב יהודה in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The finder may name the item, because the concern about a רמאי is open-ended and is not taken into account.

steps.title: The משנה seems to fit רב יהודה and not רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a claimant who names the item but gives no סימנים, and uses it to challenge רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if he named the lost item but did not give its סימנים, the finder should not give it to him. This makes sense if the finder announces only 'a lost item.' Then the משנה is teaching that even if the claimant correctly says 'a cloak,' we do not return it without סימנים. But if the finder announces 'a cloak,' then the finder said 'cloak' and the claimant said 'cloak.' Does the משנה really need to tell us that without סימנים we do not return it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging רב נחמן from the משנה's wording. If the finder already announced 'a cloak,' the משנה's rule would be too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רב יהודה, the claimant who says 'cloak' has guessed correctly, so we might think that is enough. The משנה is needed to teach that it is not. Under רב נחמן, the claimant only repeated what he heard, so of course that proves nothing. That makes the משנה's statement look unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense if you say...
Does it need to be said? (meaning it is too obvious)

phrases.english: We learned: if he stated what the lost item is
but did not state its identifying marks,
the finder should not give it to him.
It makes sense if you say he announces 'a lost item,'
then this is what the משנה teaches us:
even though the claimant said 'a cloak,'
when he did not give identifying marks
we do not return it to him.
But if you say he announces 'a cloak,'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אִיהוּ גְּלִימָא, וְאָמַר אִיהוּ גְּלִימָא,
phrases.english: then he said 'cloak' and he said 'cloak,'
phrases.notes: The first 'he' is the finder who announced it, and the second 'he' is the claimant who just repeated it.

phrases.english: does it need to be said

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לָא אָמַר סִימָנִין לָא מַהְדְּרִינַן לֵיהּ?
phrases.english: that when he did not give identifying marks we do not return it to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the רב יהודה / רב נחמן argument against the משנה's wording
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's view that the finder announces 'a cloak'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the item was already named in the announcement, repeating its name proves nothing, so the משנה's rule would be obvious and unneeded.

steps.title: רב ספרא: the claimant gave marks, but not clear-cut ones
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא defends רב נחמן. He reads 'did not state its marks' as 'did not state its clear-cut marks.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: really, the finder announces 'a cloak.' The finder said 'cloak' and the claimant gave סימנים. So what does 'he did not state its סימנים' mean? He did not give its clear-cut סימנים.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא answers the challenge and keeps רב נחמן's view. He explains that the משנה is talking about a claimant who gave weak סימנים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case is no longer 'no marks at all.' It is 'marks that are not clear-cut,' meaning marks that many items could have. The משנה teaches something new: weak סימנים do not prove ownership. So the משנה is no longer obvious, and רב נחמן stands.

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
Really, he announces 'a cloak,'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אִיהוּ גְּלִימָא, וְאָמַר אִיהוּ סִימָנִין.
phrases.english: the finder said 'cloak,' and the claimant gave marks.
And what does 'he did not state its marks' mean?
He did not state its clear-cut marks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רב נחמן
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is about a claimant with no סימנים at all, which would be obvious under רב נחמן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a claimant whose סימנים are not clear-cut, so it teaches a new point and fits רב נחמן.
steps.whatToRemember: Under רב נחמן as explained by רב ספרא, weak, non-distinctive סימנים are not enough to get a lost item back.

steps.title: Once swindlers multiplied, claimants had to bring witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's רמאי line and brings a ברייתא: at first סימנים were enough, but later the חכמים required witnesses that the claimant is not a רמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: a swindler does not get it, even if he gives its סימנים. The רבנן taught: at first, anyone who lost an item would give סימנים and take it. Once swindlers multiplied, they enacted that we tell him: go bring witnesses that you are not a swindler, and take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה, about the רמאי. It brings a ברייתא describing a תקנה that changed how lost items are returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first, giving סימנים was enough. When swindlers became common, the חכמים added a requirement: the claimant must also bring witnesses that he is not a known swindler. This explains in practice how a רמאי is kept from getting the item.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָרַמַּאי אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמַר אֶת סִימָנֶיהָ –
phrases.english: And the swindler, even though he stated its marks,
the finder should not give it to him.
The רבנן taught: at first,
anyone who lost an item
would give marks and take it.
Once the swindlers multiplied,
they enacted that people should say to him:
Go and bring witnesses
that you are not a swindler, and take it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the announcement debate to the משנה's רמאי clause
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once swindlers became common, a claimant must bring witnesses that he is not a רמאי before he gets the item.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the rules for returning lost items can be tightened by a תקנה when people start abusing the system.
steps.confusionAlert: The witnesses do not testify that the item is his. The סימנים still do that. The witnesses only confirm that he is not a known swindler.

steps.title: The story of רב פפא's father and his lost donkey
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא applies the תקנה to רב פפא's father. The witnesses give a confusing 'yes,' then explain what they meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the case of רב פפא's father. He lost a donkey and people found it. He came before רבה בר רב הונא, who told him: go bring witnesses that you are not a swindler, and take it. He went and brought witnesses. רבה בר רב הונא asked them: do you know him to be a swindler? They said: yes. He said to them: I am a swindler?! They told him: we meant to say, 'you are not a swindler.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real story showing the witness תקנה being used. It also sets up a problem: the witnesses' answer sounded like it went against the claimant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story confirms that בית דין actually required these witnesses. The witnesses answered 'yes' to 'is he a swindler,' which sounds damaging. They then said they meant 'yes, he is not a swindler.' This sets up the question of whether to trust their correction.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this case (introduces a supporting story)

phrases.english: Like that case of the father of Rav Pappa,
he lost a donkey, and others found it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: He came before Rabba bar Rav Huna.
He said to him: Go bring witnesses
that you are not a swindler, and take it.
He went and brought witnesses.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: יָדְעִיתוּן בֵּיהּ דְּרַמַּאי הוּא?
phrases.english: He said to them: Do you know about him that he is a swindler?
They said to him: Yes.
He said to them: I am a swindler?!
phrases.notes: This is רב פפא's father speaking, shocked at his own witnesses.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: אֲנַן ״לָאו רַמַּאי אַתְּ״ קָאָמְרִינַן.
phrases.english: They said to him: We were saying 'you are not a swindler.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the ברייתא's witness תקנה with a real case
steps.raayaObject: The תקנה that a claimant must bring witnesses that he is not a רמאי
steps.raayaSupportSource: A case before רבה בר רב הונא involving רב פפא's father

steps.title: A person doesn't bring witnesses against himself
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא rules that the witnesses' correction is believable, because no one brings witnesses who will hurt his own case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: it makes sense that they meant he is not a swindler, because a person does not bring guilt upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא decides how to read the confusing testimony. He accepts that the witnesses meant to support the claimant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claimant chose these witnesses himself. No one would bring witnesses whom he knows will call him a swindler. So the witnesses' 'yes' must have been a misunderstanding, and their correction is accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is reasonable / it makes sense
Guilt / something that counts against him

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא: מִסְתַּבְּרָא,
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said: It makes sense,
a person does not bring guilt upon himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִסְתַּבְּרָא, לָא מַיְיתֵי אִינִישׁ חוֹבְתָּא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the confusion raised in the story
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Witnesses whom a claimant brings himself are understood as supporting him, because a person does not bring testimony against himself.
steps.whatToRemember: Today a claimant needs both סימנים and witnesses that he is not a רמאי. If those witnesses answer in a confusing way, we assume they meant to help the person who brought them.

steps.title: A working animal is kept and a non-working animal is sold
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a found animal that earns its keep is kept and worked, and one that only eats is sold. The source is ״וַהֲשֵׁבוֹתוֹ לוֹ״, which tells the finder to think about how to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any animal that works and eats should work and eat. An animal that does not work but eats should be sold. The פסוק says 'and you shall return it to him,' which means: see how you can return it to him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It tells the finder what to do with a found animal while he waits for the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If an animal works, its work pays for its food, so keeping it costs the owner nothing. If it only eats, the owner would have to pay the finder back for all that food, and the cost could swallow the animal's value. So the finder sells it. Reading ״וַהֲשֵׁבוֹתוֹ לוֹ״ as 'see how you will return it' means the return has to actually benefit the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Works and eats; its work covers the cost of its food
'And you shall return it to him' (דברים 22:2)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule for השבת אבידה: returning an object means protecting the owner's interests. Holding on to the physical item is not enough.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Any living thing that works and eats
phrases.notes: He means an animal whose work earns enough to pay for its food.

phrases.english: shall work and eat
and a thing that does not work but eats
shall be sold
as it is said: 'and you shall return it to him'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:2

phrases.english: see how you will return it to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה begins on a new topic: caring for found animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A self-supporting found animal is kept and worked. A non-working animal is sold, based on ״וַהֲשֵׁבוֹתוֹ לוֹ״ read as 'see how you will return it.'

steps.title: May the finder use the sale money, and is he responsible for it
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks what happens to the money from selling the animal. רבי טרפון says the finder may use it, so he is responsible if it is lost. רבי עקיבא says he may not use it, so he is not responsible if it is lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: What should be done with the money? רבי טרפון says: he may use it, so if it is lost he must pay for it. רבי עקיבא says: he may not use it, so if it is lost he does not have to pay for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a follow-up question about the sale money and brings a מחלוקת between רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions tie responsibility to the right to use the money. If the finder may use it, he takes on responsibility for it, so he must pay if it is lost. The גמרא, starting at the end of this amud, works out exactly how far that responsibility goes. If he may not use it, he is only holding it for the owner, so he does not pay if it is lost.

keyTerms.meaning: Money; here, the money from selling the animal
Responsibility to pay if something is lost

steps.confusionAlert: Here רבי עקיבא's 'not responsible' does not mean the finder may be careless. It means he does not pay if the money is lost without his fault, because he was not allowed to use it.

phrases.english: What shall be done with the money?
Rabbi Tarfon says: he may use it
therefore, if it is lost, he is liable for it.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: לֹא יִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בָּהֶן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: he may not use it

phrases.aramaic: לְפִיכָךְ אִם אָבְדוּ – אֵין חַיָּיב בְּאַחְרָיוּתָן.
phrases.english: therefore, if it is lost, he is not liable for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the ruling that a non-working animal is sold: what happens to the money from the sale?
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי טרפון: the finder may use the money and is responsible for it. רבי עקיבא: he may not use it and is not responsible if it is lost.

steps.title: Must the finder care for a working animal forever
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking whether the finder must keep caring for a self-supporting animal with no time limit.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: And forever?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a short question on the first rule of the משנה. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a working animal 'works and eats' with the finder, but gave no time limit. The גמרא asks whether the finder is stuck with this job forever, which would be an unreasonable burden.

phrases.english: GEMARA: And forever?
phrases.notes: He means: must the finder keep caring for the working animal with no end?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the time limit for the משנה's first rule, the working animal.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long must the finder care for a self-supporting found animal before he may sell it?

steps.title: שמואל sets the limit at twelve months
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of שמואל answers that the finder cares for the animal for twelve months.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: until twelve months.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the finder's duty lasts twelve months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This puts a limit on the משנה's rule. After twelve months, even a working animal no longer has to be kept. The ברייתא in the next step explains what the finder does after that.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
until twelve months.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question 'forever?'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The finder cares for a self-supporting animal for twelve months.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the twelve-month limit for cows and donkeys
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same thing: a working animal like a cow or donkey is cared for twelve months. After that, the finder assesses its value and sets the money aside.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: any animal that works and eats, like a cow or a donkey, he takes care of for twelve months. From then on, he assesses its value and puts the money aside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same as שמואל, as support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא matches שמואל's twelve months and adds what happens next. After the time is up, the finder sells the animal at its proper value and keeps the money for the owner. This way the owner still gets his value back without the finder caring for the animal endlessly.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports the statement)

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
any thing that works and eats
such as a cow and a donkey

phrases.aramaic: מִטַּפֵּל בָּהֶן עַד שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ,
phrases.english: he tends to them for up to twelve months;
from then on
he assesses their value and puts it aside.
phrases.notes: He sells the animal at its value and keeps the money for the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports שמואל's answer with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's twelve-month limit for self-supporting animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating that a cow or donkey is tended for twelve months, then valued and the money set aside

steps.title: Shorter limits for calves, foals, geese and roosters
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא continues: calves and foals are cared for three months, and geese and roosters thirty days. After that, the finder assesses their value and sets the money aside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Calves and foals: he takes care of them for three months, and from then on he assesses their value and puts the money aside. Geese and roosters: he takes care of them for thirty days, and from then on he assesses their value and puts the money aside.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and gives shorter time limits for animals that do not earn their keep as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Young calves and foals cannot work yet, and birds give less in return for their food. So keeping them longer would eat up the owner's value faster, and the time limits are shorter. The ending is the same in every case: assess the value and set the money aside for the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Calves and foals (young animals that cannot work yet)

steps.whatToRemember: How long the finder must care for an animal depends on how well it pays for its own food: working animals 12 months, calves and foals 3 months, birds 30 days. After that he assesses the value, sells it, and keeps the money for the owner. This is all built on the משנה's idea of 'see how you will return it to him.'

phrases.english: Calves and foals
he tends to them for three months;
from then on, he assesses their value and puts it aside.
Geese and roosters
he tends to them for thirty days;
from then on, he assesses their value and puts it aside.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲגָלִים וּסְיָיחִין מִטַּפֵּל בָּהֶן שְׁלֹשָׁה חֳדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with time limits for other kinds of animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Calves and foals are tended for three months, and geese and roosters for thirty days. After that they are valued and the money is set aside for the owner.

steps.title: A hen is treated like a large animal
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק rules that a hen has the same status as a בהמה גסה, so the finder cares for it for twelve months.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק says: A hen is like a large animal.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק adds a new ruling: a found hen is handled like a cow or donkey, not like the smaller birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ברייתא gave geese and roosters only thirty days, so we might have thought a hen gets a short time too. רב נחמן בר יצחק puts the hen in the twelve-month group instead.

keyTerms.meaning: A large animal, like a cow or donkey
Like; has the same law as

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up תַּרְנְגוֹלֶת (a hen) with תַּרְנְגוֹלִין (roosters). The hen gets twelve months. Roosters get a much shorter time.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says:
A hen is like a large animal.
phrases.notes: He means the finder cares for a hen for twelve months, just like a cow or donkey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new animal, the hen, to the twelve-month group from step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A found hen is cared for twelve months, like a בהמה גסה.

steps.title: A second teaching supports the hen ruling and gives other time limits
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports רב נחמן בר יצחק: a hen and a large animal get twelve months. It then gives calves and foals thirty days, and geese, roosters and any costly animal three days.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught so: A hen and a large animal are cared for twelve months, and after that he assesses their value and sets the money aside. Calves and foals are cared for thirty days, and after that he assesses their value and sets the money aside. Geese, roosters, and anything whose care costs more than it earns are cared for three days, and after that he assesses their value and sets the money aside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רב נחמן בר יצחק said about the hen. The same ברייתא also lists other animals with shorter times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is the first line, which puts the hen together with the large animal for twelve months. The rest of the ברייתא gives thirty days for calves and three days for geese and roosters. These numbers do not match the first ברייתא from steps 24-25, which sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא (a supporting source)
From here on; after that time
He assesses their value and puts the money aside for the owner
Its care costs more than what it earns

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule about care costing more than earnings explains the whole list. The less an animal pays its own way, the sooner the finder may sell it.

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
A hen and a large animal –
he takes care of them for twelve months;
from then on, he assesses their value and sets it aside.
phrases.notes: He sells the animals and keeps the money safe for the owner.

phrases.english: Calves and foals –
he takes care of them for thirty days;
from then on, he assesses their value and sets it aside.
Geese and roosters
and anything whose care costs more than what it brings in –
he takes care of them for three days;
from then on, he assesses their value and sets it aside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 26 with a ברייתא that says the same thing.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's ruling that a hen is like a בהמה גסה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that lists the hen together with the large animal for twelve months

steps.title: The two teachings clash on calves and on geese
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the two ברייתות disagree. Calves and foals get three months in one and thirty days in the other. Geese and roosters get thirty days in one and three days in the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is difficult: the ruling on calves and foals contradicts the other ruling on calves and foals, and the ruling on geese and roosters contradicts the other ruling on geese and roosters!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts the two ברייתות side by side and shows that their time limits do not match for the same animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 gave calves and foals three months, but the new ברייתא gives thirty days. Step 25 gave geese and roosters thirty days, but the new ברייתא gives three days. The same animal cannot have two different time limits.

keyTerms.meaning: It is difficult; there is a contradiction
Against (short for עַל); this source is set against that one

phrases.english: There is a difficulty: calves and foals against calves and foals,
phrases.notes: Step 25 said three months, but the new ברייתא says thirty days.

phrases.english: and geese and roosters against geese and roosters!
phrases.notes: One says thirty days, the other says three days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the ברייתא from step 27 with the one in step 25 and finds a clash.
steps.kashyaTarget: The time limits for calves, foals, geese and roosters in the two ברייתות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same animals get different care periods in two teachings, so they seem to contradict each other.

steps.title: Grazing calves versus fattened calves
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the calves-and-foals clash. Three months applies to young animals that graze. Thirty days applies to ones that must be fattened.
steps.simpleTranslation: Calves and foals against calves and foals is not difficult: this one is about those that graze, and that one is about those being fattened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the first clash by saying each ברייתא talks about a different kind of calf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calves that graze in the pasture are cheap to keep, so the finder keeps them three months. Calves that must be fattened take much more work and cost, so he keeps them only thirty days. This fits the rule that costly care means a shorter time.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no real contradiction
This one... and that one (each source refers to a different case)

phrases.aramaic: עֲגָלִים וּסְיָיחִין אַעֲגָלִים וּסְיָיחִין לָא קַשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Calves and foals against calves and foals is not difficult:
this one is about those that graze,
phrases.notes: This is the three-month ruling from step 25.

phrases.english: and that one is about those that are fattened.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲגָלִים וּסְיָיחִין אַעֲגָלִים וּסְיָיחִין לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of the קשיא in step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each source speaks of a different situation)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות seemed to speak of the same calves and foals.
steps.terutzMaskana: Grazing calves get three months. Calves that need fattening get thirty days.

steps.title: Large geese versus small geese
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the geese-and-roosters clash. Thirty days applies to large ones, and three days applies to small ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Geese and roosters against geese and roosters is also not difficult: this one is about large ones, that one is about small ones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second clash the same way, by splitting the birds into large and small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Large geese and roosters are easier to care for, so the finder keeps them thirty days. Small ones need much more effort, so he keeps them only three days. Both ברייתות are now correct, each for its own case.
steps.whatToRemember: Hens and large animals get twelve months. Grazing calves and foals get three months, and fattened ones get thirty days. Large geese and roosters get thirty days, and small ones get three days. The more costly the care, the sooner the finder may sell.

phrases.aramaic: אֲווֹזִין וְתַרְנְגוֹלִין אַאֲווֹזִין וְתַרְנְגוֹלִין נָמֵי לָא קַשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Geese and roosters against geese and roosters is also not difficult:
this one is about large ones,
phrases.notes: This is the thirty-day ruling from step 25.

phrases.english: that one is about small ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲווֹזִין וְתַרְנְגוֹלִין אַאֲווֹזִין וְתַרְנְגוֹלִין נָמֵי לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second half of the קשיא in step 28, using the same method as step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the size of the bird
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות seemed to speak of the same geese and roosters.
steps.terutzMaskana: Large geese and roosters get thirty days. Small ones get three days.

steps.title: Do not let the food eat up the animal's value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule about an animal that eats but does not work. A ברייתא then explains, from "וַהֲשֵׁבוֹתוֹ לוֹ", that the finder must not spend a calf's worth feeding calves, or a goose's worth feeding geese.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said an animal that does not work but does eat should be sold. The רבנן taught: "And you shall return it to him" means: make sure you can actually return it to him. Do not feed away the value of a calf on the calves, a foal on the foals, a goose on the geese, or a rooster on the roosters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה and brings a ברייתא that explains the reason behind it: the finder's job is to return something real to the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק does not only say "return it." It is read as "see how you return it," meaning return it in a way that leaves the owner with value. If the finder keeps feeding the animals until their food has cost as much as an animal is worth, the owner ends up with nothing. That is why such an animal is sold.

keyTerms.meaning: "And you shall return it to him". The פסוק about returning a lost object.
See how you will return it. Make sure the return is worth something.

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא gives the reason behind all the time limits in the earlier steps. Once caring for the animal would use up its value, the finder must sell it.

phrases.english: And one that does not work but eats.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה, which says such an animal should be sold.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"And you shall return it to him"
phrases.notes: דברים 22:2

phrases.english: See how you will return it to him,
that he should not feed a calf to calves,
phrases.notes: He means: don't spend a whole calf's worth of money feeding the lost calves.

phrases.english: and a foal to foals,
a goose to geese,
and a rooster to roosters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the time limits for caring for animals to the next line of the משנה and its source in the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A finder must not keep feeding found animals until their value is used up; the פסוק requires a return that leaves the owner with value.

steps.title: What happens to the money from the sale
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה: what is done with the money from selling the animal. רבי טרפון says the finder may use it, and the משנה continues with רבי עקיבא's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: What should be done with the money? רבי טרפון says: he may use it, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה to begin discussing it. This is a setup for the analysis that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the animal is sold, the finder is holding money instead of an animal. רבי טרפון allows him to use it, so he must pay it back if it is lost. The "etc." points to רבי עקיבא, who says he may not use it, so he is not responsible if it is lost.

keyTerms.meaning: Money, the value received from the sale
A תנא who allows the finder to use the money
"Etc.", a sign that the rest of the quoted text continues

steps.confusionAlert: Being allowed to use the money is not only a benefit for the finder. Because he may use it, he also becomes responsible to pay it back if it gets lost.

phrases.english: What shall be done with the money?
Rabbi Tarfon says: he may use it, etc.
phrases.notes: The "etc." stands for the rest of the משנה, where רבי עקיבא says he may not use it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new section: the גמרא moves from caring for the animal to the money from its sale.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי טרפון permits the finder to use the sale money (and so he is responsible for it); רבי עקיבא forbids using it.

steps.title: Narrowing down what the dispute is about
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to point out the exact limits of the disagreement between רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא. The sentence continues in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree only...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting to pin down exactly where רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא disagree. This line sets up the next move, which continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase עַד כָּאן לָא פְּלִיגִי means "they only disagree as far as this." It marks the edge of the argument, so the גמרא can show what both תנאים would agree on. The full point and its use come in the next part.

keyTerms.meaning: "They only disagree up to here". This marks how far a dispute goes.

phrases.english: They disagree only...
phrases.notes: Literally "up to here they do not disagree." The sentence is finished in the next part of the גמרא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins analyzing the dispute quoted in step 32 by marking where it stops.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The גמרא begins to mark how far the dispute between רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא reaches.
